review_basis: Original numbered AIF module 03 WebP slides 19, 20 and 21 individually inspected. Labeled-data regression and classification examples, plots and k-NN diagrams read in visual order.

scenes.title: Supervised learning: learn from labeled examples
scenes.narration: Start at the heading, supervised learning: learn from labeled examples. Supervised does not mean that a teacher watches every prediction. It means that during training, we give the computer examples with the correct answer already attached. The slide splits into two side-by-side paths. On the left, regression predicts a continuous number, such as a house's sale price. Step one shows a small table. A home with one thousand square feet sold for two hundred thousand US dollars; a home with fifteen hundred square feet sold for three hundred thousand; and a home with two thousand square feet sold for four hundred thousand. These numbers are synthetic teaching examples, not actual home valuations. In step two, follow the arrow into the graph. The horizontal axis is floor area in square feet, and the vertical axis is sale price in US dollars. The line illustrates a learned relationship: larger floor area is associated with a higher sale price in these examples. Step three is a trained model, a learned mapping from input to output. In step four, a new home with twelve hundred fifty square feet enters, and the model estimates approximately two hundred fifty thousand dollars. That is inference: using a trained model on something it has not previously seen. Notice that an estimate can be wrong, because real house prices also depend on location, condition and other factors. Now follow the purple path on the right. Classification predicts a category, not an amount. Three labeled messages are provided: a project meeting and an invoice are not spam, while claim your prize now is spam. The training algorithm looks for useful patterns in the messages, illustrated by the words prize, win, cash and meeting. The trained classifier receives a new message, win cash today, and predicts the category spam. A word alone is not proof of spam, and responsible systems check error rates. The key choice is between the type of answer: a number such as a price suggests regression; a category such as spam or not spam suggests classification. Quick check: if a college wants to predict a student's numerical exam score, which side would we choose? Regression. If it wants to decide pass or fail, which side? Classification, because pass and fail are categories. Remember the bottom warning: these data are illustrative, and collecting trustworthy labels may require considerable human work.

scenes.title: Supervised Learning – Regression
scenes.narration: This slide zooms in on regression. Begin with the numbered explanation on the left. Regression predicts a numeric value, often called a continuous target. Continuous does not mean the system is perfectly precise; it means the answer is a quantity, not a named class. Training uses historical examples that contain both inputs and known outcomes, and the algorithm searches for a useful pattern. A customer might ask, how much will this house sell for? That is different from asking, is this email spam? In the center, follow the diagram from input features through the trained regression model to its output. Features are pieces of information we supply to the model. Here they include house size in square feet and location, such as a neighborhood. The output is a predicted house price. The graph below reinforces the idea. The horizontal axis represents house size, the vertical axis represents house price, and yellow dots represent observed examples. The upward blue line summarizes the learned trend. The dots do not all sit on the line, so a prediction is not a certainty. Even with a good general trend, individual homes can cost more or less than expected. On the right, the presentation deliberately contrasts classification. The input is an email saying get cheap medications now, and the trained classification model produces a label, spam or not spam. The two worked examples below show a project update marked not spam and a promotional message marked spam. These are example outcomes rather than guaranteed classifications. Look back to the left-hand common examples: house prices and temperatures are quantities. An email category is a discrete label. In an exam scenario, read the requested output first. If the question asks how many, how much or what temperature, regression is often the natural choice. If it asks which category, choose classification. A model still needs representative data, proper evaluation and monitoring for mistakes. Can a regression model predict whether an email is spam simply by outputting a price-like number? Not directly. The required output is a class, so a classifier is the more direct fit.

scenes.title: Classification: binary, multiclass and multilabel
scenes.narration: This visual introduces three kinds of classification. Read the upper row from left to right. Binary classification means choosing between two categories. The left card shows an email promising a free phone and asking for an immediate click. The illustrated output is spam, with spam and not spam as the two possible answers. A cautious system should not assume any single phrase always determines the class. The middle card is multiclass classification: the prediction is one category from three or more mutually exclusive choices. The example uses an animal photograph and the labels mammal, bird and reptile. The dog image is predicted as mammal. One point to notice: multiclass does not mean that every category is correct at the same time; the system chooses a single class for this example. The right-hand card changes the rule. Multilabel classification permits zero, one or several categories at once. One movie can be both action and comedy, while other possible genres include drama and science fiction. Each applicable genre can be selected independently. Now move to the lower left, k-nearest neighbors, often shortened to k N N. Think of placing a new student into a club based on the most similar past students. Here the axes are example features such as weight and height, each point represents a labeled example, and the white star represents a new input. With k equal to three, the algorithm looks at the three closest labeled points and chooses the most common class among them. The slide says two out of the three nearest neighbors are mammals, so the predicted class is mammal. Similarity depends on the features and distance rule; it is not a guarantee the classification is correct. The bottom middle shows where classification helps: identifying suspicious transactions, estimating whether a customer will leave, labeling an image, and directing a support ticket to the right department. Finally, the bottom-right box repeats the distinction. Classification predicts a discrete category. Regression predicts a continuous numerical amount. Here is a decision check. A film can be tagged both educational and comedy. Would we use multiclass or multilabel? Multilabel, because more than one category may apply to the same film. If an application must choose exactly one department for a support ticket, multiclass is a sensible design.
